title: Why prices move
desc: A market is a non-stop auction, and prices move on surprises

cards.title: Ten buyers, one seller
cards.situation: You own 1 share. The last trade was $50. Ten people want to buy it right now, and nobody else is selling. What do you do?
cards.added: Scene written for the app; idea from p.7 (design board OLD Ch1 L1, the auction lesson)

visual.label: Ten buyers want your one share. The last trade was $50

options.feedback: Ten buyers, one share: they have to outbid each other. If the deal happens at $52, your app now shows $52. That’s how a price rises.

options.text: Sell at $50 to the first person
options.feedback: Ten buyers want one share, so someone will pay $51 or $52. Selling at $50 leaves that money with the buyer.

options.text: Wait for the exchange to set a new price
options.feedback: Nobody sets prices from above. The exchange only records where a buyer and a seller agree. That deal becomes the price.

cards.work: 10 buyers, 1 share: offers climb $50 → $51 → $52. The deal at $52 becomes the price.

cards.title: A market is a non-stop auction
cards.text: When you buy a share, someone else sold it to you. Every trade has two sides, and the price on your screen is just **the most recent deal** they agreed on. No magic, no secret room.

visual.title: Three deals in a row
visual.label: Three deals: $50, then $51, then $52. Each one becomes the price on the screen

blocks.tip: More buyers than sellers? Buyers offer more and the price **rises**. Sellers in a hurry? They accept less and it **falls**.

cards.title: Record profits, falling price?
cards.added: $10M / $8M numbers (book gives the idea only, p.7)
cards.text: Everyone expects a company to earn $10 million. It earns $8 million: a record, but less than hoped. The stock **falls**. Prices don’t move on good or bad news. They move on news that is **better or worse than people expected**.

visual.title: Company profit this year
visual.label: Investors expected $10 million profit; the company earned $8 million, a record, and the stock fell 6%

blocks.tip: A great company can fall on great news if everyone expected amazing news.

cards.title: Which way does the price go?
cards.q: Drag each situation into the right box.
cards.added: Sort built from p.7 ideas; numbers added

itemFeedback.Expected profit $5M, actual $6M: $6M beat the $5M people expected. A good surprise pushes the price up.
itemFeedback.Expected profit $10M, actual $8M: A record that misses expectations is a letdown. The price falls.
itemFeedback.Sellers rush to get out: Sellers in a hurry accept less, so each new deal prints lower.

cards.right: Beat the forecast: up. Missed it, even with a record: down. Sellers in a hurry: down.
cards.work: $6M vs $5M expected: beat, up. $8M vs $10M expected: miss, down.

cards.title: Record profits, falling stock
cards.q: A company reports record profits. Its stock falls 6% the same day. What best explains it?

options.feedback: Prices move on the gap between results and expectations. If people hoped for more, a record is still a letdown.

options.text: Market makers decided to lower the price
options.feedback: Nobody decides the price. It’s the last deal between a buyer and a seller, and here sellers outnumbered buyers.

options.text: Too many people wanted to buy
options.feedback: More buyers would push the price up, not down. A 6% fall means sellers outnumbered buyers.

options.text: The company created more shares that day
options.feedback: Nothing in the story says new shares. Look for the surprise: results versus what was expected.

cards.work: Expected more than the record → a letdown → more sellers → price −6%.

cards.headline: You know where every price comes from.
lines: A price is the last deal between a buyer and a seller.
More buyers push prices up; sellers in a hurry push them down.
Prices move on surprises versus expectations, not on good or bad headlines.
